claim: The climate is becoming more variable and the frequency of floods and droughts is increasing according to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
source: Research by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) indicates that the climate is becoming more variable and that the frequency of floods and droughts is increasing (IPCC, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to IPCC, 2013.

claim: Elevated temperatures combined with periods of drought represent a major threat to food security.
source: Elevated temperatures combined with periods of drought represent a major threat to food security (Sreenivasulu et al., 2007; Barnabas et al., 2008; Brutnell and Frommer, 2012; Sreenivasulu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Abscisic acid (ABA) has been found in all kingdoms of life, including plant saprophytic and pathogenic fungi, animals such as sponges (Axinella polypoides) and hydroids (Eudendrium racemosum), and human parasites (Toxoplasma gondii).
source: Abscisic acid (ABA), a terpenoid plant hormone, has been found in all kingdoms of life, including plant saprophytic and pathogenic fungi, animals such as sponges (Axinella polypoides) and hydroids (Eudendrium racemosum), and human parasites (Toxoplasma gondii) (Crocoll et al., 1991; Nagamune et al., 2008; Li et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In plants, abscisic acid (ABA) serves as the key phytohormone produced during drought.
source: In plants, abscisic acid (ABA) serves as the key phytohormone produced during drought, and is a master regulator of water use efficiency, stomatal aperture, and other mechanisms of tolerance to drought and osmotic stress (Sreenivasulu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: ABA is a master regulator of water use efficiency, stomatal aperture, and other mechanisms of tolerance to drought and osmotic stress.
source: In plants, abscisic acid (ABA) serves as the key phytohormone produced during drought, and is a master regulator of water use efficiency, stomatal aperture, and other mechanisms of tolerance to drought and osmotic stress (Sreenivasulu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: ABA controls seed dormancy and germination.
source: ABA also controls seed dormancy and germination (Finkelstein and Rock, 2002; Bentsink and Koornneef, 2008; Kanno et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: ABA is perceived by a family of ABA receptors (PYR/PYL/RCAR proteins).
source: ABA is perceived by a family of ABA receptors (PYR/PYL/RCAR proteins, Ma et al., 2009; Park et al., 2009), which then bind to and prevent ABA co-receptor proteins (protein phosphatase 2CA proteins, PP2CAs, Umezawa et al., 2009; Vlad et al., 2009) from deactivating Sucrose non-fermenting Related Kinase 2s (SnRK2s, Fujii and Zhu, 2009; Fujita et al., 2009; Nakashima et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: PYR/PYL/RCAR proteins bind to and prevent ABA co-receptor proteins (protein phosphatase 2CA proteins, PP2CAs) from deactivating Sucrose non-fermenting Related Kinase 2s (SnRK2s).
source: ABA is perceived by a family of ABA receptors (PYR/PYL/RCAR proteins, Ma et al., 2009; Park et al., 2009), which then bind to and prevent ABA co-receptor proteins (protein phosphatase 2CA proteins, PP2CAs, Umezawa et al., 2009; Vlad et al., 2009) from deactivating Sucrose non-fermenting Related Kinase 2s (SnRK2s, Fujii and Zhu, 2009; Fujita et al., 2009; Nakashima et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The increase in SnRK2 activity triggers phosphorylation of transcription factors and transporters.
source: The resulting increase in SnRK2 activity triggers phosphorylation of transcription factors (Yoshida et al., 2010) and transporters (Geiger et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2009; Sato et al., 2009), and affects ABA-dependent responses that vary with respect to cell type and developmental or environmental context.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Only approximately 25% of the ABA responsive transcripts in leaves are also ABA responsive in guard cells.
source: For example, only ∼25% of the ABA responsive transcripts in leaves are also ABA responsive in guard cells (Wang et al., 2011), and ABA signaling specifically in the endodermis promotes lateral root quiescence in plants exposed to salt stress (Duan et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: ABA signaling specifically in the endodermis promotes lateral root quiescence in plants exposed to salt stress.
source: For example, only ∼25% of the ABA responsive transcripts in leaves are also ABA responsive in guard cells (Wang et al., 2011), and ABA signaling specifically in the endodermis promotes lateral root quiescence in plants exposed to salt stress (Duan et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: ABA accumulation under stress conditions is controlled at the level of biosynthesis, catabolism, and transport as well as through reversible conversion to ABA-glucose ester.
source: ABA accumulation under stress conditions is controlled at the level of biosynthesis, catabolism, and transport as well as through reversible conversion to ABA-glucose ester, an inactive form of ABA potentially used in both storage and long distance transport (Cutler and Krochko, 1999; Seo and Koshiba, 2002; Wilkinson and Davies, 2002; Nambara and Marion-Poll, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: ABA-glucose ester is an inactive form of ABA potentially used in both storage and long distance transport.
source: ABA accumulation under stress conditions is controlled at the level of biosynthesis, catabolism, and transport as well as through reversible conversion to ABA-glucose ester, an inactive form of ABA potentially used in both storage and long distance transport (Cutler and Krochko, 1999; Seo and Koshiba, 2002; Wilkinson and Davies, 2002; Nambara and Marion-Poll, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Many of the enzymes involved in ABA metabolism have been identified, some of which are present as multi-gene families.
source: Many of the enzymes involved in ABA metabolism have been identified, some of which are present as multi-gene families (Tan et al., 2003; Kushiro et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The weak acid properties of ABA (pKa 4.7) led to the hypothesis that ABA diffuses freely across membranes in its undissociated lipophilic form.
source: The weak acid properties of ABA (pKa 4.7) led to the hypothesis that ABA diffuses freely across membranes in its undissociated lipophilic form (Kaiser and Hartung, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Subsequent studies implicated cellular uptake via transport proteins.
source: Subsequent studies implicated cellular uptake via transport proteins (Astle and Rubery, 1985b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Functional studies identified proteins that can mediate transport of ABA.
source: Over the past few years, functional studies identified proteins that can mediate transport of ABA (Kang et al., 2010; Kuromori et al., 2010, 2011; Kanno et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: FRET sensors are fusion proteins that report target molecule interactions through changes in the conformation of intrinsic sensory domains.
source: FRET sensors are fusion proteins that report target molecule interactions through changes in the conformation of intrinsic sensory domains.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the nature of FRET sensors based on established knowledge.

claim: Conformational changes in FRET sensors affect the efficiency of energy transfer from a fused FRET donor fluorescent protein to a fused FRET acceptor fluorescent protein.
source: These conformational changes affect the efficiency of energy transfer from a fused FRET donor fluorescent protein to a fused FRET acceptor fluorescent protein.
evidence: This is a direct statement about how FRET sensors work based on established knowledge.

claim: Changes in energy transfer in FRET sensors can be detected by measuring changes in the relative intensity of the two fluorescent proteins (ratio change) after excitation of the donor.
source: Changes in energy transfer can be detected by measuring changes in the relative intensity of the two fluorescent proteins (ratio change) after excitation of the donor; the ratio change reports target molecule concentration.
evidence: This is a direct statement about how FRET sensors are measured based on established knowledge.

claim: FRET sensors have been used in plant tissues to study calcium and zinc dynamics with subcellular spatial and near real-time temporal resolution.
source: FRET sensors have been used in plant tissues to study calcium and zinc dynamics with subcellular spatial and near real-time temporal resolution (e.g., Krebs et al., 2012; Lanquar et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Metabolite dynamics have been studied using FRET sensors leading to the characterization of sugar transport in roots of intact seedlings.
source: Metabolite dynamics have also been studied using FRET sensors leading to, for example, the characterization of sugar transport in roots of intact seedlings (Deuschle et al., 2006; Chaudhuri et al., 2008, 2011; Grossmann et al., 2011; Grossmann et al., 2012) and the identification of novel sugar transporters (Chen et al., 2010, 2012; Xuan et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: FRET sensors have led to the identification of novel sugar transporters.
source: Metabolite dynamics have also been studied using FRET sensors leading to, for example, the characterization of sugar transport in roots of intact seedlings (Deuschle et al., 2006; Chaudhuri et al., 2008, 2011; Grossmann et al., 2011; Grossmann et al., 2012) and the identification of novel sugar transporters (Chen et al., 2010, 2012; Xuan et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: ABACUS1 is an Abscisic Acid Concentration and Uptake Sensor version 1 that reports ABA levels.
source: Here we developed a combinatorial and iterative engineering platform for FRET sensors that led to the identification of ABACUS1, an Abscisic Acid Concentration and Uptake Sensor version 1 that reports ABA levels.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the development and function of ABACUS1.

claim: ABACUS1 is specific for ABA.
source: The combinatorial screening of the Destination vector series and the Entry clone library allowed for rapid testing of hundreds of constructs and led to the identification of ABACUS1, which is specific for ABA and is optimized for reduced size, fluorophore brightness and photostability, and high ratio change (i.e. high signal-to-noise).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the specificity of ABACUS1 based on experimental data.

claim: ABACUS1 is optimized for reduced size, fluorophore brightness and photostability, and high ratio change.
source: The combinatorial screening of the Destination vector series and the Entry clone library allowed for rapid testing of hundreds of constructs and led to the identification of ABACUS1, which is specific for ABA and is optimized for reduced size, fluorophore brightness and photostability, and high ratio change (i.e. high signal-to-noise).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the optimization of ABACUS1 based on experimental data.

claim: ABACUS1 variants cover a broad detection range for in vivo use.
source: We then generated ABACUS1 variants covering a broad detection range for in vivo use.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the generation of ABACUS1 variants.

claim: When expressed in yeast, ABACUS1 detected concentrative ABA uptake mediated by the AIT1/NRT1.2 transporter.
source: When expressed in yeast, ABACUS1 detected concentrative ABA uptake mediated by the AIT1/NRT1.2 transporter.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results with ABACUS1 in yeast.

claim: Arabidopsis roots expressing ABACUS1-2µ (Kd∼2 µM) and ABACUS1-80µ (Kd∼80 µM) respond to perfusion with ABA in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Arabidopsis roots expressing ABACUS1-2µ (Kd∼2 µM) and ABACUS1-80µ (Kd∼80 µM) respond to perfusion with ABA in a concentration-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results with ABACUS1 in Arabidopsis roots.

claim: The properties of the observed ABA accumulation in roots appear incompatible with the activity of known ABA transporters (AIT1, ABCG40).
source: The properties of the observed ABA accumulation in roots appear incompatible with the activity of known ABA transporters (AIT1, ABCG40).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the interpretation of experimental results.

claim: ABACUS reveals effects of external ABA on homeostasis, that is, ABA-triggered induction of ABA degradation, modification, or compartmentation.
source: ABACUS reveals effects of external ABA on homeostasis, that is, ABA-triggered induction of ABA degradation, modification, or compartmentation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about findings from ABACUS experiments.

claim: Time-course analysis of ABACUS responses demonstrated negative regulation of cytosolic ABA levels by ABA.
source: ABA feedback on ABA levels was identified as a potentially critical aspect of ABA signaling as time-course analysis of ABACUS responses demonstrated negative regulation of cytosolic ABA levels by ABA.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental findings.

claim: Potential ABA sensory domains (PAS) were selected from members of ABA co-receptor complexes; specifically, nine members of the PYR/PYL/RCAR family of ABA receptors and three members of the PP2CA sub-family of ABA co-receptor phosphatases from Arabidopsis.
source: To generate FRET sensors for ABA, potential ABA sensory domains (PAS) were selected from members of ABA co-receptor complexes; specifically, nine members of the PYR/PYL/RCAR family of ABA receptors and three members of the PP2CA sub-family of ABA co-receptor phosphatases from Arabidopsis (Table 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Two types of sensors were generated: single domain sensors in which either a PYR/PYL/RCAR or PP2CA polypeptide alone (sPAS) is sandwiched between two fluorescent proteins, or double domain sensors, in which a PYL/PYR/RCAR fused via a linker to a PP2CA (dPAS) is sandwiched between two fluorescent proteins.
source: We generated two types of sensors: single domain sensors in which either a PYR/PYL/RCAR or PP2CA polypeptide alone (sPAS) is sandwiched between two fluorescent proteins, or double domain sensors, in which a PYL/PYR/RCAR fused via a linker to a PP2CA (dPAS) is sandwiched between two fluorescent proteins (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: More than 50 sPAS and dPAS variants were engineered.
source: To cover a large test space of ABA sensory domains, we engineered sensor constructs using >50 sPAS and dPAS variants sandwiched between a fluorescent protein FRET pair (i.e., multiple PAS Entry clones were recombined with a single destination vector (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of variants engineered.

claim: Initial experiments, in which constructs were expressed in Escherichia coli and yeast, were unsuccessful, most likely due to proteolysis of the fusion proteins.
source: Initial experiments, in which constructs were expressed in Escherichia coli and yeast, were unsuccessful, most likely due to proteolysis of the fusion proteins, as evidenced by maintenance of fluorescence but loss of FRET during cell lysis (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Proteolysis appeared specific to PAS domain sensors and was not observed for other FRET sensors.
source: Proteolysis appeared specific to PAS domain sensors and was not observed for other FRET sensors (Fehr et al., 2002, 2003; Lager et al., 2003; Okumoto et al., 2005; Gu et al., 2006; Lager et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental observations, with citations to other FRET sensors.

claim: Sensory domain proteolysis was circumvented by using a protease-deficient yeast strain (strain BJ5465 lacking Pep4 and Prb1).
source: Sensory domain proteolysis was circumvented by using a protease-deficient yeast strain (strain BJ5465 lacking Pep4 and Prb1, Figure 2) for expression and purification.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental approach, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Four out of 15 sPAS sensors showed a relatively small ratio change (∼1.06–1.12) in response to addition of 200 µM (±)-ABA.
source: Four out of 15 sPAS sensors showed a relatively small ratio change (∼1.06–1.12) in response to addition of 200 µM (±)-ABA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: dPAS sensors containing both partners of an ABA co-receptor complex might exhibit larger ABA-dependent ratio changes due to larger conformational changes triggered by ABA-dependent intra-molecular interactions between two ABA binding domains.
source: We hypothesized that dPAS sensors containing both partners of an ABA co-receptor complex might exhibit larger ABA-dependent ratio changes due to larger conformational changes triggered by ABA-dependent intra-molecular interactions between two ABA binding domains.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a hypothesis.

claim: The presence of both ABA interaction domains may increase ABA affinity, as demonstrated for PYR/PYL/RCAR affinity in the presence of PP2CA co-receptors.
source: The presence of both ABA interaction domains may also increase ABA affinity, as demonstrated for PYR/PYL/RCAR affinity in the presence of PP2CA co-receptors (Santiago et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a hypothesis, with a citation to supporting research.

claim: ABI1aid fused to PYL1 (dPAS110) consistently yielded comparatively large ratio changes in response to ABA (ΔDxAm/DxDm ∼1.29 to 1.63).
source: Among these combinations, ABI1aid fused to PYL1 (dPAS110) consistently yielded comparatively large ratio changes in response to ABA (ΔDxAm/DxDm ∼1.29 to 1.63; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Linkers can have dramatic effects on sensor responses.
source: Linkers can have dramatic effects on sensor responses (Deuschle et al., 2005b; Hires et al., 2008; Takanaga et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: FRET pair variants containing enhanced dimerization versions of the fluorescent proteins were consistently ABA responsive.
source: Many of the sensor variants did not show responses to ABA addition, however FRET pair variants containing enhanced dimerization versions of the fluorescent proteins were consistently ABA responsive (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to figures.

claim: dPAS110 with L12 and L118 linkers showed large ABA-triggered responses when fused to the edAphrodite.t9/t7.ed.eCFP.t9 pair.
source: As seen before, dPAS110 with L12 and L118 linkers showed large ABA-triggered responses when fused to the edAphrodite.t9/t7.ed.eCFP.t9 pair; notably the other three linker variants also showed ABA responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: dPAS110 fused by linkers L52 or L118 containing the elastic GPGGA-repeat and sandwiched by edCitrine/edCerulean yielded the highest ratio change.
source: dPAS110 fused by linkers L52 or L118 containing the elastic GPGGA-repeat (i.e. molecular spring motif, Grashoff et al., 2010) and sandwiched by edCitrine/edCerulean yielded the highest ratio change (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to figures.

claim: dPAS110.L52.DR38, a fusion protein harboring edCerulean/edCitrine, the ABA interaction domain of a PP2CA ABA co-receptor (ABI1aid), an ABA receptor (PYL1), and three distinct linkers connecting the domains (attB1, L52, attB2), was named Abscisic Acid Concentration and Uptake Sensor version 1 (ABACUS1).
source: dPAS110.L52.DR38, a fusion protein harboring edCerulean/edCitrine (pDR FLIP38), the ABA interaction domain of a PP2CA ABA co-receptor (ABI1aid), an ABA receptor (PYL1), and three distinct linkers connecting the domains (attB1, L52, attB2), was named Abscisic Acid Concentration and Uptake Sensor version 1 (ABACUS1, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the naming of ABACUS1, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: In ABACUS1, the binding of ABA to PYR/PYL/RCAR receptor proteins and the ABA-dependent interaction of PYR/PYL/RCARs with PP2CA phosphatases is co-opted to drive an ABA-dependent structural change in the fusion protein, which increases energy transfer between donor and acceptor and results in a positive ratio change.
source: In ABACUS1, the binding of ABA to PYR/PYL/RCAR receptor proteins and the ABA-dependent interaction of PYR/PYL/RCARs with PP2CA phosphatases is co-opted to drive an ABA-dependent structural change in the fusion protein, which increases energy transfer between donor and acceptor and results in a positive ratio change.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the mechanism of ABACUS1.

claim: The increase in energy transfer in ABACUS1 did not occur with the metabolic precursor xanthine, other plant hormones, or other ions and metabolites tested.
source: This increase in energy transfer did not occur with the metabolic precursor xanthine, other plant hormones, or other ions and metabolites tested (Figure 3B–D), but was also induced by the ABA analog pyrabactin (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to figures.

claim: The increase in energy transfer in ABACUS1 was induced by the ABA analog pyrabactin.
source: This increase in energy transfer did not occur with the metabolic precursor xanthine, other plant hormones, or other ions and metabolites tested (Figure 3B–D), but was also induced by the ABA analog pyrabactin (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to Figure 3E.

claim: The ratio change in ABACUS1 was proportional to the ABA concentration.
source: The ratio change was proportional to the ABA concentration (Figure 4); the prototype ABACUS1 is characterized by an apparent affinity of ∼80 µM for (+)-ABA, and thus is referred to here as ABACUS1-80µ (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: The prototype ABACUS1 is characterized by an apparent affinity of ∼80 µM for (+)-ABA.
source: The ratio change was proportional to the ABA concentration (Figure 4); the prototype ABACUS1 is characterized by an apparent affinity of ∼80 µM for (+)-ABA, and thus is referred to here as ABACUS1-80µ (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Mutation of histidine-60 to proline switches PYR1 from a dimer to a monomer and increases its affinity for ABA.
source: Mutation of histidine-60 to proline switches PYR1 from a dimer to a monomer and increases its affinity for ABA (Dupeux et al., 2011); the corresponding mutation in the PYL1 moiety of ABACUS1-80µ produced ABACUS1-2µ, a variant with a higher affinity for ABA of ∼2 µM (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research and experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The corresponding mutation in the PYL1 moiety of ABACUS1-80µ produced ABACUS1-2µ, a variant with a higher affinity for ABA of ∼2 µM.
source: Mutation of histidine-60 to proline switches PYR1 from a dimer to a monomer and increases its affinity for ABA (Dupeux et al., 2011); the corresponding mutation in the PYL1 moiety of ABACUS1-80µ produced ABACUS1-2µ, a variant with a higher affinity for ABA of ∼2 µM (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Disruption of the ABA binding pocket of PYL1 by mutation of the ABA coordinating lysine-86 to alanine abrogates ABA binding.
source: Disruption of the ABA binding pocket of PYL1 by mutation of the ABA coordinating lysine-86 to alanine abrogates ABA binding (Melcher et al., 2009); the corresponding mutation in ABACUS1-80µ resulted in a non-responsive variant ABACUS1-nr (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research and experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The corresponding mutation in ABACUS1-80µ resulted in a non-responsive variant ABACUS1-nr.
source: Disruption of the ABA binding pocket of PYL1 by mutation of the ABA coordinating lysine-86 to alanine abrogates ABA binding (Melcher et al., 2009); the corresponding mutation in ABACUS1-80µ resulted in a non-responsive variant ABACUS1-nr (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Mutation of ABI1 tryptophan-300 to alanine abrogates its interaction with ABA and the PYL1 binding pocket.
source: Mutation of ABI1 tryptophan-300 to alanine abrogates its interaction with ABA and the PYL1 binding pocket (Melcher et al., 2009); the respective mutation in ABACUS1-80µ (ABACUS1-W300A) showed a reduced ratio change in response to ABA, but surprisingly no reduction in affinity (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research and experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The respective mutation in ABACUS1-80µ (ABACUS1-W300A) showed a reduced ratio change in response to ABA, but surprisingly no reduction in affinity.
source: Mutation of ABI1 tryptophan-300 to alanine abrogates its interaction with ABA and the PYL1 binding pocket (Melcher et al., 2009); the respective mutation in ABACUS1-80µ (ABACUS1-W300A) showed a reduced ratio change in response to ABA, but surprisingly no reduction in affinity (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: ABA binding to PYL1 determines the apparent Kd, whereas the formation of the ABA-PYL1-ABI1 ternary complex is required for a maximal ratio change in ABACUS1-80µ.
source: This finding indicates that ABA binding to PYL1 determines the apparent Kd, whereas the formation of the ABA-PYL1-ABI1 ternary complex is required for a maximal ratio change in ABACUS1-80µ.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the interpretation of experimental results.

claim: A histidine-142 to alanine mutation in the ABA binding pocket of PYL1 is known to reduce ABA affinity.
source: Finally, a histidine-142 to alanine mutation in the ABA binding pocket of PYL1, which is known to reduce ABA affinity (Melcher et al., 2009), resulted in a drastically reduced affinity in ABACUS1-H142A (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research and experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: A histidine-142 to alanine mutation in ABACUS1-80µ resulted in a drastically reduced affinity in ABACUS1-H142A.
source: Finally, a histidine-142 to alanine mutation in the ABA binding pocket of PYL1, which is known to reduce ABA affinity (Melcher et al., 2009), resulted in a drastically reduced affinity in ABACUS1-H142A (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: The linear detection range of FRET sensors with a single binding site covers approximately two orders of magnitude.
source: The linear detection range of FRET sensors with a single binding site covers approximately two orders of magnitude; ABACUS1-2µ and ABACUS1-80µ together cover an overlapping range from ∼200 nM to 800 µM (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the properties of FRET sensors, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: ABACUS1-2µ and ABACUS1-80µ together cover an overlapping range from ∼200 nM to 800 µM.
source: The linear detection range of FRET sensors with a single binding site covers approximately two orders of magnitude; ABACUS1-2µ and ABACUS1-80µ together cover an overlapping range from ∼200 nM to 800 µM (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Yeast two-hybrid interaction screens can be used as an indirect way of monitoring ABA transport.
source: Yeast two-hybrid interaction screens can be used as an indirect way of monitoring ABA transport.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a method based on established knowledge.

claim: When supplied exogenously with ≥10 µM ABA, the ABA uptake activity (through endogenous transporters) of yeast reaches high enough levels to allow detection of ABA-mediated yeast two-hybrid interactions between the ABA co-receptor components PYR/PYL/RCAR and PP2CAs.
source: When supplied exogenously with ≥10 µM ABA, the ABA uptake activity (through endogenous transporters) of yeast reaches high enough levels to allow detection of ABA-mediated yeast two-hybrid interactions between the ABA co-receptor components PYR/PYL/RCAR and PP2CAs (Park et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: At reduced ABA levels, the ABA-mediated interaction is not detectable.
source: At reduced ABA levels, the ABA-mediated interaction is not detectable (Kanno et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: A screen at low ABA levels had successfully been used to identify members of the nitrate/peptide transporter superfamily as putative ABA importers.
source: A screen at low ABA levels had successfully been used to identify members of the nitrate/peptide transporter superfamily as putative ABA importers (Kanno et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Yeast cells did not accumulate sufficient ABA to induce a ratio change in ABACUS1-2µ even at 20 µM exogenous (±)-ABA.
source: Yeast cells did not accumulate sufficient ABA to induce a ratio change in ABACUS1-2µ even at 20 µM exogenous (±)-ABA (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: Expression of the high affinity ABA importer AIT1/NRT1.2 conferred ABA transport activity as detected by DxAm/DxDm ratio change of ABACUS1-2µ and ABACUS1-80µ sensors.
source: However, expression of the high affinity ABA importer AIT1/NRT1.2 conferred ABA transport activity as detected by DxAm/DxDm ratio change of ABACUS1-2µ and ABACUS1-80µ sensors (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: ABACUS1-2µ exhibited a near maximal ratio change in response to exogenous ABA supplied well below the sensor's apparent Kd of 2 µM (+)-ABA, suggesting that AIT1/NRT1.2 concentrates ABA against an ABA gradient.
source: ABACUS1-2µ exhibited a near maximal ratio change in response to exogenous ABA supplied well below the sensor's apparent Kd of 2 µM (+)-ABA, suggesting that AIT1/NRT1.2 concentrates ABA against an ABA gradient.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results and their interpretation.

claim: FRET sensor expression under control of the CaMV 35S promoter has been shown to be subject to gene silencing.
source: FRET sensor expression under control of the CaMV 35S promoter has been shown to be subject to gene silencing (Deuschle et al., 2006; Krebs et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Sensor silencing was reduced in the rdr6-11 gene silencing mutant of Arabidopsis.
source: Sensor silencing was reduced in the rdr6-11 gene silencing mutant of Arabidopsis (Peragine et al., 2004; Deuschle et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: When FRET calcium sensors were expressed from the UBQ10 promoter, silencing in wild type (Col0) plants was reduced.
source: When FRET calcium sensors were expressed from the UBQ10 promoter, silencing in wild type (Col0) plants was reduced (Krebs et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Significant levels of ABACUS1 fluorescence were detectable only in the rdr6 silencing mutant.
source: However, as observed for other FRET sensors (Deuschle et al., 2006; Chaudhuri et al., 2008; Lanquar et al., 2014), significant levels of ABACUS1 fluorescence were detectable only in the rdr6 silencing mutant.
evidence: This is a direct statement about experimental results, with citations to other FRET sensors.

claim: Confocal microscopy showed bright fluorescence from the sensors, which lacked subcellular targeting sequences, in the cytosol of roots, hypocotyls and leaves.
